item.title: Forty Uzbeks to train as chefs to Japanese standards for employment in Japan
item.description: Migration Agency: the programme runs in two stages — six months of Japanese language and cooking in Uzbekistan, then one year of practice in Japan and a state-recognised licence.

item.title: America's first Muslim senator Abdul El-Sayed launches ‘Habibi PAC’
item.description: Days after his historic win, the first Muslim US senator announced a leadership committee to raise money for other candidates.

item.title: How to vote in the United States: registering and voting for new citizens
item.description: To vote in the U.S. you must first register (except in North Dakota). Only U.S. citizens who are 18 by Election Day and residents of their state may vote. A newly naturalized citizen can register the day of the ceremony. There are four ways to register: online, by mail (the National Mail Voter Registration Form), in person, or at the DMV (the 1993 National Voter Registration Act — "motor voter"). Deadlines vary by state. Based on official sources (vote.gov, USCIS, the Election Assistance Commission).

item.title: Zelensky: Russia fired a North Korean KN-23 missile at Kyiv
item.description: Ukraine's president said 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones hit Kyiv overnight and that a North Korean missile struck one of the energy facilities.

item.title: The founding of Uzbekistan Airways (1992): the independent state's national airline
item.description: The national airline Uzbekistan Airways was established on 28 January 1992 and took over the operations of Aeroflot's Uzbekistan division on 31 May 1992. It was among the first carriers in the former USSR to switch to Western-built aircraft: in 1993 it acquired its first Airbus A310-300s and opened routes to Frankfurt and Bangkok. Its base is Tashkent (today Islam Karimov Tashkent International Airport). The fleet was later renewed with the Boeing 767 and then the Boeing 787-8 (first 787 in August 2016). The airline became one of the symbols of independent Uzbekistan's air links with the world. Based on official and open sources.

item.title: How OPEC works and how oil prices are set
item.description: OPEC — the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries — was founded on 14 September 1960 in Baghdad by five states (Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela); its headquarters has been in Vienna since 1 September 1965. As of 2026 it has 11 member states (the United Arab Emirates left in 2026). OPEC members hold about 79.5% of the world's proven oil reserves and about 38% of production (2022). The group influences the market through production quotas; since 2016 it coordinates with countries such as Russia and Kazakhstan in the "OPEC+" format. Based on official sources.

item.title: Qatari plan: if Iran accepts nuclear inspections, the Strait of Hormuz reopens
item.description: The Guardian: Qatar is pressing Iran to let UN inspectors into its bombed nuclear sites; in return the US would lift its blockade and release $8bn.

item.title: Jehovah's Witnesses ease 81-year blood-transfusion ban, 23 days after a member's death
item.description: BBC: Isaac Valdez, 26, died after refusing a blood transfusion on religious grounds; 23 days later the Governing Body changed the rule.

item.title: The Central Asian Arabs: Uzbekistan's oldest, almost vanished community
item.description: The Central Asian Arabs are an ethnic Arab community that settled in Transoxiana in several waves between the 7th and 17th centuries, starting with the Arab conquest. They lived in Samarkand, Bukhara, Qashqadaryo and Surxondaryo (present-day Uzbekistan) and Khatlon (Tajikistan). Their total number today is no more than 10,000; Uzbekistan's 1989 census recorded 2,800 (another figure gives 12,880), and Tajikistan's 2010 census over 4,000. Their language — Central Asian Arabic — is endangered. Most have gradually assimilated into the Uzbek and Tajik populations. Based on scholarly sources.

item.title: Two experienced skydivers die in a midair collision in California
item.description: Two licensed skydivers collided at about 150 feet while preparing to land at Skydive Elsinore in Lake Elsinore; the center said there was no sign of equipment malfunction.

item.title: On the Foundations of State Independence: 31 August 1991 and the Legal Birth of Uzbekistan
item.description: On 31 August 1991 Uzbekistan declared state independence and adopted the Constitutional Law On the Foundations of State Independence. This is a factual history of the legal foundation of independent statehood.

item.title: Uzbekistan's Central Bank raises its 2026 inflation forecast to 7%
item.description: At its November 4 meeting the Central Bank raised its end-2026 inflation forecast from 6.5% to about 7% and kept the key rate at 14%.

item.title: Mirziyoyev calls for raising remittances to $50 billion and criticizes officials
item.description: At a November 2 meeting on labor migration, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev set a goal of raising annual remittances to $50 billion and criticized officials for insufficient support to migrants.

item.title: How the Two Eids — Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha — Are Observed: The Eid Prayer, the Takbir, and Zakat al-Fitr
item.description: When the two Islamic festivals fall, how the Eid prayer is performed, and what the takbir and Zakat al-Fitr are — a facts-only explainer. (Differences between schools are shown neutrally; Uzbekistan mainly follows the Hanafi school.)

item.title: U.S. Work Authorization: How the EAD (Form I-765), Form I-9, and E-Verify Work
item.description: Who needs a U.S. work permit (EAD), how to get one, and what the employer's Form I-9 and E-Verify check are — a facts-only guide for immigrants.

item.title: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to 200 years over the deaths of 190 children
item.description: A court in Mombasa on November 6 found cult leader Paul Nthenge Mackenzie guilty of murdering 191 people in the Shakahola case and sentenced him to 200 years in prison.

item.title: US adds 165,000 jobs in October as unemployment falls to 4.1%
item.description: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the US economy added 165,000 jobs in October; the strong report is expected to influence the Federal Reserve's December decision.

item.title: The 1966 Tashkent Earthquake: The City Was Destroyed, the Whole Union Rebuilt It, and Its Population Changed
item.description: The earthquake of 26 April 1966 destroyed central Tashkent. This is a factual history of the quake, the all-Union reconstruction, and the shift in the city's demographics.

item.title: India warns students in Uzbekistan that their medical degrees may not be recognized
item.description: India's National Medical Commission and Ministry of External Affairs urged citizens to verify that medical schools in Uzbekistan meet national standards; otherwise the degree may not be recognized in India.

item.title: Uzbekistan's move to a bicameral parliament: the 2002 referendum and the creation of the Senate (2002–2005)
item.description: From 1995 Uzbekistan's Oliy Majlis was unicameral, with 250 deputies. In a referendum on 27 January 2002 voters were asked to make parliament bicameral and to extend the presidential term from five to seven years; according to official results both measures were approved. The bicameral Oliy Majlis took office on 27 January 2005 after the December 2004–January 2005 elections: a lower house, the Legislative Chamber (120 seats at first), and an upper house, the Senate (100 members). Based on reputable sources.

item.title: Adam Hamawy becomes the first Muslim elected to Congress from New Jersey
item.description: Democrat Adam Hamawy — a former army surgeon who worked in Gaza — won New Jersey's 12th district in the November 3 midterms to become the first Muslim elected to Congress from the state.

item.title: Iran's IRGC says two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on November 5. The account has not been independently verified.

item.title: Uzbekistan expands its list of banned extremist online sources to 2,057
item.description: Uzbekistan's Supreme Court updated its register of banned religious-extremist and terrorist online sources on November 3, bringing the total to 2,057. Most are social-media channels and accounts.

item.title: How the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) works
item.description: The Federal Reserve (the "Fed") is the central bank of the United States, created by the Federal Reserve Act signed by President Woodrow Wilson on 23 December 1913. It consists of the Board of Governors in Washington (7 members, 14-year terms) and 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks; monetary policy is set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Its dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices (a 2% annual inflation target adopted in January 2012). Its main tool is the federal funds rate: at the 28 October 2026 meeting it was held at 3.75–4.00%. Based on official sources (federalreserve.gov).

item.title: Digital payments in Uzbekistan: how Uzcard, Humo, Click and Payme work
item.description: Uzbekistan's cashless payment system is built on two national card schemes — Uzcard (launched in 2004) and Humo (launched by the Central Bank in 2019) — plus the mobile apps linked to them, chiefly Click and Payme. Cards are linked to an app; users send peer-to-peer (P2P) transfers by card number, pay by QR, and settle utility and other bills. Since 2021 Uzcard and Humo have become interoperable. According to a KPMG study, cashless card payments reached about 72% of GDP in 2025. Based on official and reputable sources.

item.title: Polish refugees and the Anders' Army in Uzbekistan during World War II (1941–1942)
item.description: In July 1941 the Sikorski–Mayski agreement restored Soviet–Polish relations and opened the way to forming a Polish army in the USSR. Commanded by General Władysław Anders, this army was relocated in early 1942 to Uzbekistan and other Central Asian republics, with its headquarters at Yangiyul. Thousands of Polish civilians, including many children, also came south; hunger and a typhus epidemic took many lives. Between March and September 1942 the army and civilians — about 115,000–116,000 people in all — were evacuated via Krasnovodsk to Iran. Based on reputable historical sources.

item.title: Hackers walk back claim of Uzbekistan data leak affecting 27 million
item.description: A group calling itself Butterfly first claimed it had taken the personal data of more than 27 million Uzbek citizens from a state database, then softened the claim into a "white-hat" vulnerability warning. No actual breach has been officially confirmed.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a Houthi missile fired toward Medina
item.description: The Saudi-led coalition said on November 5 that it had shot down a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis toward the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest cities.

item.title: How U.S. Bank Deposit Insurance (FDIC) Works
item.description: The FDIC is a federal system that protects a depositor's money with a government guarantee even if the bank fails. Coverage is automatic, up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category. Here is how it works.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed becomes the first Muslim US senator
item.description: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan in the November 3 midterms to become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
